Income and Renewable Heating Adoption in Switzerland

Yannik Zimmermann & Birk Diener

2026-05-20

Motivation

Switzerland has committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, with the heating sector representing one of the largest remaining sources of fossil fuel consumption. Transitioning residential buildings away from oil and gas heating towards renewable alternatives such as heat pumps, solar thermal systems, and biomass is therefore a critical lever of the energy transition. However, adoption rates of renewable heating systems vary significantly across Swiss municipalities (bfs 2024). This project investigates a potential explanation for this heterogenous adoption pattern, namely whether a statistically measurable relationship exists between community-level income and the share of renewable heating systems installed.

Project Aim

This project aims to quantify the relationship between median income at the municipality level and the share of buildings equipped with renewable heating systems across Swiss municipalities. The analysis will address two core research questions:

  • Is there a statistically significant relationship between municipal-level financial capacity, measured through taxable income, and the share of residential buildings equipped with renewable heating systems across Swiss municipalities?
  • To what extent is this relationship robust to structural characteristics of the building stock, namely the share of single-family houses and the age of the building stock, and to cantonal differences in subsidy programmes?

The analysis draws on the Federal Building and Dwellings Register (GWR) and ESTV municipal tax data. Given known data quality limitations in the GWR heating system entries, a systematic data recency assessment is integrated into the analysis prior to modelling. The findings will be visualised through choropleth maps and scatter plots to make spatial and socioeconomic patterns legible for a broader audience.

Data Sources

Two datasets are used for this analysis, both openly available and joinable at the Swiss municipality level (BFS-Gemeindecode). The first is the Federal Building and Dwellings register (GWR), which records the primary heating energy, building category, and year of construction for every residential building in Switzerland. Key variables used in this analysis are the heating system type (GWAERZH1), the energy source (GENH1), the year of construction (GBAUJ), the information source of the heating entry (GWAERSCEH1), the last update date of the heating entry (GWAERDATH1), and the municipality code (GGDENR).

While the general availability of data to answer the research question is good, there is a significant challenge regarding the reliability of the heating system entries. The last comprehensive national update of this information took place as part of the Volkszählung 2000. Since then, municipal building departments are responsible for updating entries, primarily through building permit applications. As a result, data quality varies across municipalities, and heating systems installed without a building permit — such as most external air-source heat pumps — may not be recorded. We investigate this aspect further in the data preparation chapter.

The second dataset is the income and wealth statistics from the Federal Tax Administration (ESTV), which provides median taxable income per municipality at the level of natural persons. It is published annually with a lag of approximately two years.

Approach

The analysis proceeds in four steps: First, GWR building data is aggregated to the municipality level to compute the share of residential buildings equipped with a renewable heating system as a fraction of all buildings with a recorded heating system entry. Renewable heating is defined as heat pump, solar thermal, or biomass combined with energy source. District heating is excluded from the primary definition as its adoption is structurally determined by local infrastructure rather than individual investment decisions, but is included in a sensitivity analysis. The share of pre-1980 buildings per municipality serves as the building age control variable.

Second, the municipal renewable heating share is joined to the ESTV income data using the BFS municipality code. Third, regression models are estimated using a stepwise approach: a baseline model with median income as the sole predictor, followed by successive addition of building structure controls (share of single-family houses, share of pre-1980 buildings), sociodemographic controls (municipal type, log population size), and cantonal fixed effects to absorb unobserved variation in subsidy programmes and building regulations. The municipal share of low-quality heating entries is included as a control variable throughout all model specifications. The stability of the income coefficient across specifications is reported.

Fourth, findings are visualized through choropleth maps showing the spatial distribution of renewable heating adoption and median income respectively.

Data Preparation

Before proceeding to the analysis, the GWR building data is prepared and aggregated to the municipal level. The preparation process includes filtering for residential buildings, flagging renewable heating systems, andÍ assessing the quality of the heating system entries.

Residential buildings are identified using two GWR variables. First, GKAT (building category) is restricted to codes 1020 (exclusively residential) and 1030 (residential with secondary use), excluding buildings without mostly residential use. Second, GSTAT (building status) is restricted to code 1004, retaining only buildings recorded as currently existing and excluding buildings under construction, demolished, or otherwise inactive. Together, these two filters define the analytical population of existing residential buildings on which all subsequent measures are computed.

Heating systems are categorised based on the energy source variable (GENH1) across ten mutually exclusive groups: no heating system (7500), air-source heat pump (7501), ground- and water-source heat pump (7510–7513), gas (7520), oil (7530), wood and biomass (7540–7543), waste heat (7550), electricity (7560), solar thermal (7570), district heating (7580–7582), and unspecified or other (7598–7599). A building is flagged as renewable if its primary energy source is a heat pump, solar thermal, wood or biomass, waste heat, or recorded as having no heating system. The latter category is included on the grounds that buildings without an active heating system generate no fossil fuel consumption from space heating, making their exclusion from the renewable count methodologically conservative. District heating is retained as a separate flag for sensitivity analysis, as its adoption depends on local infrastructure availability rather than individual investment decisions.

## 1. Read the GWR building data --------------------------------------------
# The file is tab-separated even though it ends in .csv. We only read the
# columns we actually use (the full file has ~50 columns and ~3.3 M rows).

buildings <- read_tsv(
  here("gwr", "gebaeude_batiment_edificio.csv"),
  col_select = c(GGDENR, GGDENAME, GDEKT,
                 GKAT, GKLAS, GSTAT, GBAUJ,
                 GWAERZH1, GENH1, GWAERSCEH1, GWAERDATH1),
  na = c("", "NA"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

## 2. Keep only existing residential buildings -----------------------------
# GKAT: 1020 = exclusively residential, 1030 = residential with side use
# GSTAT 1004 = the building actually exists today.

residential <- buildings %>%
  filter(GKAT %in% c(1020, 1030), GSTAT == 1004)


## 3. Flag each building --------------------------------------------------
# Renewable heating per the project brief:

residential <- residential %>%
  mutate(
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Heizsystem-Kategorien — GENH1
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    is_no_heatsystem = GENH1 == 7500,
    is_hp_air        = GENH1 == 7501,
    is_hp_ground     = GENH1 %in% c(7510, 7511, 7512, 7513),
    is_gas           = GENH1 == 7520,
    is_oil           = GENH1 == 7530,
    is_wood          = GENH1 %in% c(7540, 7541, 7542, 7543),
    is_waste_heat    = GENH1 == 7550,
    is_electric      = GENH1 == 7560,
    is_solar         = GENH1 == 7570,
    is_district      = GENH1 %in% c(7580, 7581, 7582),
    is_other         = GENH1 %in% c(7598, 7599),

    # Aggregierte Heizsystem-Flags
    is_heatpump      = is_hp_air | is_hp_ground,
    is_renewable     = is_heatpump | is_wood | is_solar |
                       is_waste_heat | is_no_heatsystem,

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Gebäudestruktur
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    is_efh           = GKLAS == 1110,

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Gebäudealter — Flags und Faktorvariable
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    is_pre1945       = !is.na(GBAUJ) & GBAUJ < 1945,
    is_postwar       = !is.na(GBAUJ) & GBAUJ >= 1945 & GBAUJ < 1981,
    is_transition    = !is.na(GBAUJ) & GBAUJ >= 1981 & GBAUJ < 2001,
    is_modern        = !is.na(GBAUJ) & GBAUJ >= 2001 & GBAUJ < 2021,
    is_new           = !is.na(GBAUJ) & GBAUJ >= 2021,
    is_age_unknown   = is.na(GBAUJ),

    building_epoch   = factor(
      case_when(
        is.na(GBAUJ)   ~ "unknown",
        GBAUJ < 1945   ~ "pre1945",
        GBAUJ < 1981   ~ "postwar",
        GBAUJ < 2001   ~ "transition",
        GBAUJ < 2021   ~ "modern",
        TRUE           ~ "new"
      ),
      levels = c("pre1945", "postwar", "transition", "modern", "new", "unknown")
    ),

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Datenqualität
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    is_lowqual       = GWAERSCEH1 == 860 | is.na(GWAERDATH1)
  )

residential <- residential %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("is_"), ~ coalesce(.x, FALSE)))

## 5. Aggregate to the municipality ---------------------------------------
# Renewable share is defined over buildings with a heating entry, so the
# denominator is sum(!is.na(GWAERZH1)), not n().

muni <- residential %>%
  group_by(bfs_id = GGDENR, municipality = GGDENAME, canton = GDEKT) %>%
  summarise(
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Grundzahlen
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    n_buildings          = n(),
    n_missing_heating    = sum(is.na(GENH1)),

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Heizsystem-Anteile (Nenner: alle Gebäude)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    share_renewable      = sum(is_renewable)  / n(),
    share_heatpump       = sum(is_heatpump)   / n(),
    share_hp_air         = sum(is_hp_air)     / n(),
    share_hp_ground      = sum(is_hp_ground)  / n(),
    share_solar          = sum(is_solar)      / n(),
    share_wood           = sum(is_wood)       / n(),
    share_waste_heat     = sum(is_waste_heat) / n(),
    share_oil            = sum(is_oil)        / n(),
    share_gas            = sum(is_gas)        / n(),
    share_electric       = sum(is_electric)   / n(),
    share_district       = sum(is_district)   / n(),
    share_other          = sum(is_other)      / n(),

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Gebäudestruktur (Nenner: alle Gebäude)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    share_efh            = sum(is_efh)        / n(),

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Gebäudealter (Nenner: alle Gebäude)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    share_pre1945        = sum(is_pre1945)    / n(),
    share_postwar        = sum(is_postwar)    / n(),
    share_transition     = sum(is_transition) / n(),
    share_modern         = sum(is_modern)     / n(),
    share_new            = sum(is_new)        / n(),
    share_age_unknown    = sum(is_age_unknown) / n(),

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Datenqualität (Nenner: alle Gebäude)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    share_lowqual        = sum(is_lowqual)    / n(),

    .groups = "drop"
  )

Unfortunately, the heating system entries in the GWR are of limited reliability. The last comprehensive national update of this information took place as part of the Volkszählung 2000, and since then, municipal building departments are responsible for updating entries, primarily through building permit applications. As a result, data quality varies across municipalities, and heating systems installed without a building permit — such as most external air-source heat pumps — may not be recorded. This is visible in Figure 1, which plots the most recent update year of the heating entry per building: approximately 600,000 residential buildings have not had their heating entry updated since 2000, and a further 1.08 million buildings have no update date recorded at all. Together these two groups represent approximately 50% of the 3.3 million buildings in the GWR.

## 4. Quick data-quality check --------------------------------------------
# When was the heating entry last updated? The brief notes this is a problem,
# many entries still go back to the 2000 census.

residential %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(substr(GWAERDATH1, 1, 4))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(year), year >= 1990) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Latest update of the GWR heating entry",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of buildings") +
  theme_minimal()

Figure 1: Distribution of GWR heating entry update years for residential buildings in Switzerland

Note: The figure shows the number of residential buildings by the year of their most recent heating system entry update (GWAERDATH1). Buildings with no recorded update date (n = 1,083,361) are excluded from the plot. The spike in 2001 reflects entries sourced from the Volkszählung 2000 (GWAERSCEH1 = 860), which represent the last comprehensive national update of heating system data. The subsequent increase from 2019 onwards reflects growing administrative activity following the 2017 revision of the GWR ordinance, which made heating data recording mandatory for new building permits.

To account for this, each building is assigned a binary low-quality flag if its heating entry either has no recorded update date or is explicitly sourced from the Volkszählung 2000 (GWAERSCEH1 = 860). Aggregated to the municipal level, this produces a share of low-quality heating entries per municipality, which is used as a control variable in the regression models. The median municipality has 58% of its heating entries flagged as low quality, with an interquartile range of 48.5% to 69.3%, indicating that the data quality challenge is structural rather than isolated. Results should therefore be interpreted as conservative estimates: low-quality entries are likely concentrated in older building stock that is disproportionately fossil-heated, meaning the measured renewable heating shares likely underestimate true adoption rates, and any detected income effect is likely attenuated by this noise rather than inflated.

estv_file <- here("estv", "statistik-dbst-np-kennzahlen-mit-2022.xlsx")

income <- read_excel(
  estv_file,
  sheet = "Gemeinden - Communes",
  na    = c("", "NA", "-")
) %>%
  select(bfs_id = 3, median_income = median_steink) %>%
  filter(!is.na(bfs_id))

muni_joined <- muni %>%
  left_join(income, by = "bfs_id")

muni_analysis <- muni_joined %>%
  filter(!is.na(median_income))

Of the 2,110 municipalities in the analytical sample, 12 could not be matched to ESTV income data, most likely due to municipal mergers where GWR and ESTV use different reference dates for municipality codes. These municipalities are excluded from the regression analysis, leaving a final sample of 2,098 municipalities.

## STATPOP — Einwohnerzahl pro Gemeinde
statpop <- read_delim(
  here("gwr", "STATPOP2024_GMDE.csv"),
  delim = ";",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  select(bfs_id = GMDE, pop_total = BBTOT)

## Raumgliederungen — Gemeindetypologie
raumgliederung <- read_excel(
  here("gwr", "Raumgliederungen.xlsx"),
  skip = 2,
  col_names = c("bfs_id", "muni_name", "canton_id", "canton",
                "district_id", "district", "typology_3",
                "typology_9", "typology_25")
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(bfs_id)) %>%
  select(bfs_id, typology_3, typology_9, typology_25) %>%
  mutate(
    bfs_id     = as.numeric(bfs_id),
    typology_3 = as.integer(typology_3),
    typology_9 = as.integer(typology_9),
    typology_25 = as.integer(typology_25)
  )

muni_analysis <- muni_analysis %>%
  left_join(statpop,       by = "bfs_id") %>%
  left_join(raumgliederung, by = "bfs_id") %>%
  mutate(log_pop = log(pop_total))

Analysis

## ── EDA ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

## 1. Univariate Statistiken ---------------------------------------------------
muni_analysis %>%
  select(share_renewable, median_income, share_efh,
         share_lowqual, log_pop) %>%
  summary()
##  share_renewable  median_income      share_efh      share_lowqual   
##  Min.   :0.0136   Min.   :  6900   Min.   :0.1153   Min.   :0.0000  
##  1st Qu.:0.1621   1st Qu.: 54800   1st Qu.:0.6069   1st Qu.:0.1830  
##  Median :0.2548   Median : 59700   Median :0.7002   Median :0.3181  
##  Mean   :0.2837   Mean   : 61003   Mean   :0.6794   Mean   :0.3431  
##  3rd Qu.:0.3745   3rd Qu.: 65688   3rd Qu.:0.7686   3rd Qu.:0.5101  
##  Max.   :0.9355   Max.   :115300   Max.   :0.9750   Max.   :0.9135  
##     log_pop      
##  Min.   : 3.466  
##  1st Qu.: 6.678  
##  Median : 7.457  
##  Mean   : 7.499  
##  3rd Qu.: 8.354  
##  Max.   :12.987

Univariate Statistics

The dependent variable share_renewable is right-skewed (Median 25.5%, Mean 28.4%, IQR 16.2–37.5%). The majority of municipalities fall between a 15% and 35% share of renewable heating, while a long right-hand tail extends up to 93.6%. The distribution is not skewed enough to warrant a log transformation but should be treated as a proportion during model interpretation.

Median income (median_income) is approximately symmetrically distributed (Median 59,700 CHF, IQR 54,800–65,688 CHF) with a slight right-hand tail reaching up to 115,300 CHF – driven by high-income, tax-advantaged municipalities, primarily in Zug and Schwyz. A log transformation is plausible for the regression here, as the distribution at the lower end (from approx. 30,000 CHF downwards) exhibits stronger left-skewness. The minimum of 6,900 CHF is likely due to isolated micro-municipalities with unreliable FTA (ESTV) entries.

The share of single-family houses (share_efh) varies considerably across municipalities (Median 70.0%, IQR 60.7–76.9%, Min 11.5%, Max 97.5%). Urban centres such as Zurich or Geneva fall at the lower end of the distribution, where multi-family buildings dominate the housing stock, while small rural municipalities consist almost entirely of detached housing. The positive correlation with share_renewable (r = 0.15) is in the expected direction: municipalities with a higher share of single-family houses tend to show higher renewable heating adoption, consistent with heat pumps and wood heating being predominantly installed in detached buildings.

The share of low-quality GWR heating entries (share_lowqual, Median 31.8%, IQR 18.3–51.0%) confirms the challenge outlined in the data description: one-third of the entries are outdated or undated. The wide dispersion indicates that using this share as a control variable is sensible, as it absorbs measurement noise at the municipal level.

## 2. Korrelationsmatrix -------------------------------------------------------
muni_analysis %>%
  select(share_renewable, median_income, share_efh,
         share_pre1945, share_lowqual, log_pop) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>%
  round(2)
##                 share_renewable median_income share_efh share_pre1945
## share_renewable            1.00         -0.36      0.15         -0.04
## median_income             -0.36          1.00      0.19          0.07
## share_efh                  0.15          0.19      1.00         -0.05
## share_pre1945             -0.04          0.07     -0.05          1.00
## share_lowqual             -0.02         -0.13      0.06          0.06
## log_pop                   -0.39          0.13     -0.31         -0.15
##                 share_lowqual log_pop
## share_renewable         -0.02   -0.39
## median_income           -0.13    0.13
## share_efh                0.06   -0.31
## share_pre1945            0.06   -0.15
## share_lowqual            1.00   -0.15
## log_pop                 -0.15    1.00

Correlation Matrix

The most striking finding in the correlation matrix is the negative correlation between median income and the share of renewable heating (r = –0.36). This contradicts the intuitive expectation that higher purchasing power facilitates the adoption of renewable heating systems. This effect is explained by the urban concentration of high-income municipalities: due to structural factors, urban municipalities have lower renewable shares—gas heating and district heating (excluded here) dominate—but above-average incomes.

The share of single-family houses (share_efh) is positively correlated with share_renewable (r = 0.15) and median_income (r = 0.19), and negatively correlated with log_pop (r = –0.31), confirming that larger, denser municipalities have fewer single-family houses and lower renewable shares. This pattern suggests that share_efh partially mediates the relationship between urbanity and renewable adoption, and its inclusion in the regression will help disentangle the income effect from building stock composition.

Also relevant is the negative correlation between municipality size (log_pop) and the renewable share (r = –0.39). Larger municipalities rely more heavily on fossil fuels. Since income and population size are weakly positively correlated (r = 0.13), potential multicollinearity exists, though it is non-critical at this level.

share_pre1945 shows virtually no correlation with share_renewable (r = –0.04), which is surprising at first glance, as older buildings typically have lower renovation rates. A possible explanation: in municipalities with a high share of old buildings, the GWR data entries are also older, potentially biasing the measured renewable rate upward (outdated entries may fail to classify electric heating as fossil-fuel-based, for example). The low correlation of share_lowqual with all other variables (max. |r| = 0.15) suggests that data quality issues are not systematically related to income, supporting its use as a control variable.

## 3. Plot 1 — Verteilung share_renewable -------------------------------------
p1 <- muni_analysis %>%
  ggplot(aes(share_renewable)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of renewable heating share",
    x     = "Share of buildings with renewable heating",
    y     = "Number of municipalities"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p1

Distribution of share_renewable (Histogram)

The distribution shows a clear peak at 15–30%, with the highest concentration between 10% and 35%. Only a few municipalities exceed 50%, and the tail beyond 75% likely represents small alpine municipalities with a high share of wood heating. The histogram supports using the untransformed variable as the outcome, given that the skewness is moderate. A beta regression or an arcsine transformation would be indicated if there were a stronger concentration at the boundaries (near 0 or 1), which is not the case here.

## 4. Plot 2 — Verteilung median_income ----------------------------------------
p2 <- muni_analysis %>%
  ggplot(aes(median_income)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(suffix = " CHF")) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of median taxable income",
    x     = "Median taxable income (CHF)",
    y     = "Number of municipalities"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p2

Distribution of median_income (Histogram)

The income distribution is unimodal and approximately normally distributed in its core range (40,000–80,000 CHF), with a right-hand tail caused by low-tax municipalities. The sharp drop-off below 30,000 CHF reflects the Swiss price level; outliers below this threshold require methodological verification. For the regression, a robustness check using log-transformed income is recommended: the relationship between purchasing power and adoption behavior is plausibly non-linear (each additional franc has a stronger impact at lower income levels than at higher ones).

## 5. Plot 3 — Scatterplot median_income vs. share_renewable -------------------
typology_labels <- c("1" = "Urban", "2" = "Periurban", "3" = "Rural")

p3 <- muni_analysis %>%
  mutate(typology_3 = factor(typology_3, labels = typology_labels)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(median_income, share_renewable, colour = typology_3)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(suffix = " CHF")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    title   = "Median income vs. renewable heating share",
    x       = "Median taxable income (CHF)",
    y       = "Share of buildings with renewable heating",
    colour  = "Municipality type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p3
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Scatterplot: Income vs. Renewable Share by Municipality Type

The scatterplot yields the central finding of the EDA. Three patterns stand out:

Direction: The relationship is negative across all three municipality types—as income increases, the share of renewable heating decreases. The OLS regression lines consistently display a negative slope, which is steepest for rural municipalities (green).

Level Differences: At any given income level, rural municipalities (green) have a significantly higher renewable share than peri-urban (orange) and urban municipalities (blue). At around 55,000–65,000 CHF, rural municipalities sit approximately 15–25 percentage points above the urban level. This reflects a structural composition difference: wood heating and heat pumps in detached single-family homes dominate the rural building stock.

Dispersion: The very wide dispersion—particularly in rural areas—shows that income alone explains only a fraction of the variance. This is consistent with r = –0.36. For the regression, this implies that further explanatory power must be derived from control variables and canton fixed effects.

Interpretation of the negative direction: The surprising negative sign is highly likely a composition effect: high-income municipalities are disproportionately urban (higher log_pop, more gas/district heating), while lower-income municipalities are disproportionately rural (more wood, heat pumps in single-family homes). Whether income exerts a true causal effect on heating adoption—independent of urbanity and building structure—will be revealed by the regression with controls.

## 6. Plot 4 — Boxplot share_renewable nach typology_3 ------------------------
p4 <- muni_analysis %>%
  mutate(typology_3 = factor(typology_3, labels = typology_labels)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(typology_3, share_renewable, fill = typology_3)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    title = "Renewable heating share by municipality type",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Share of buildings with renewable heating"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p4

Boxplot: Renewables by Municipality Type

The boxplot confirms the typological gradient: rural municipalities (median ~33%) > peri-urban (median ~23%) > urban (median ~15%). The IQR for rural municipalities (approx. 25–47%) is considerably wider than that of urban ones (~10–25%), indicating greater heterogeneity in rural areas—likely due to cantonal differences in subsidy regimes and local fuel availability (wood vs. heat pump potential).

Upper outliers are present across all typologies; for rural municipalities, they extend beyond 90%—representing individual alpine communities with historically established shares of wood heating. Urban outliers above 50% are rare and warrant an individual municipality-level inspection (e.g., municipalities with local heat pump programs or erroneous GWR entries).

# Nutze most_recent = TRUE, damit R die aktuellsten verfügbaren Karten zieht
gemeinden_sf <- bfs_get_base_maps(geom = "polg", most_recent = TRUE) 
kantone_sf   <- bfs_get_base_maps(geom = "kant", most_recent = TRUE) 

# Falls das klappt, kannst du direkt mit dem Join weitermachen:
map_data <- gemeinden_sf %>%
  mutate(id = as.numeric(id)) %>% 
  left_join(muni_analysis, by = c("id" = "bfs_id"))

# Gemeinsames Theme für beide Karten
map_theme <- theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position      = "right",
    legend.key.height    = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    legend.key.width     = unit(0.35, "cm"),
    plot.title           = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 6)),
    plot.margin          = margin(5, 5, 5, 5)
  )

# Karte 1 — Anteil erneuerbare Heizungen
p_map_renewable <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = map_data,
          aes(fill = share_renewable),
          colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = kantone_sf,
          fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option   = "mako",
    direction = -1,
    labels   = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    na.value = "grey88",

Choropleth Maps: Renewable Share and Median Income

The spatial distribution of renewable heating adoption (Figure X) reveals a pronounced cantonal pattern that mirrors the regression findings. Municipalities with the highest renewable shares — shown in dark blue — are concentrated in central Switzerland, particularly in the cantons of Lucerne, Zug, and parts of Solothurn and Aargau, as well as in scattered alpine municipalities across Graubünden and Valais where wood heating is historically dominant. Western Switzerland (Romandy) and Ticino show consistently lower renewable shares, displayed in light green, suggesting a structural east-west divide that likely reflects differences in cantonal subsidy regimes, building traditions, and energy infrastructure.

The income map (Figure Y) shows a complementary but inverse pattern. The highest median incomes — in dark purple — are concentrated in the greater Zurich area, the canton of Zug, and the lakeside municipalities of Geneva and Vaud. These high-income clusters correspond spatially to areas of moderate to low renewable heating adoption in the first map, providing a direct visual confirmation of the negative income–renewables correlation identified in the regression. Conversely, lower-income municipalities in Valais, Ticino, and rural peripheral regions tend to appear in warmer orange tones in the income map, while displaying comparatively higher renewable shares in the first map, consistent with the wood heating patterns of lower-income rural areas.

Juxtaposing both maps makes the composition effect discussed in the regression analysis spatially legible: the negative association between income and renewable heating is not driven by a uniform within-canton pattern, but largely by the structural contrast between high-income urban and peri-urban agglomerations on the one hand and lower-income rural municipalities on the other. The substantial cantonal variation visible in both maps — particularly the sharp contrast between neighbouring cantons along the Mittelland — underscores why cantonal fixed effects absorb a large share of the explained variance in M4.

# M1: Baseline
m1 <- lm(share_renewable ~ median_income + share_lowqual,
         data = muni_analysis)

# M2: + Gebäudestruktur
m2 <- lm(share_renewable ~ median_income + share_lowqual +
           share_efh + share_pre1945,
         data = muni_analysis)

# M3: + Soziodemografie
m3 <- lm(share_renewable ~ median_income + share_lowqual +
           share_efh + share_pre1945 +
           factor(typology_3) + log_pop,
         data = muni_analysis)

# M4: + Kantons-Fixed-Effects (via fixest für robuste SEs)
m4 <- feols(share_renewable ~ median_income + share_lowqual +
              share_efh + share_pre1945 +
              factor(typology_3) + log_pop | canton,
            data = muni_analysis,
            vcov = "hetero")

Regression Results

Across all four model specifications, the income coefficient is negative and statistically significant at the 0.1% level, confirming the negative association observed in the EDA. The magnitude and interpretation of the effect evolves substantially as controls are added.

In the baseline model (M1), a 10,000 CHF increase in median municipal income is associated with a 5.4 percentage point reduction in the renewable heating share. Adding building stock controls in M2 slightly increases the magnitude to 6.1 percentage points. The direction of this change reflects a suppressor effect: share_efh is positively correlated with both income and renewable adoption, so controlling for it reveals a stronger direct income effect. The share of single-family houses itself is strongly positive (0.295, p < 0.001), confirming that municipalities with more detached housing have substantially higher renewable shares.

In M3, the income coefficient attenuates to –4.2 percentage points per 10,000 CHF after adding municipality type and log population. This attenuation confirms the composition hypothesis from the EDA: a substantial part of the raw negative income correlation was driven by the urban-rural gradient rather than income per se. The typology dummies show a large structural gradient—rural municipalities have an 11.1 percentage point higher renewable share than urban municipalities of comparable income and building stock, and peri-urban municipalities sit 4.2 percentage points higher.

The most notable finding is the jump in R² from 32.3% (M3) to 57.7% (M4) when cantonal fixed effects are added, while the income coefficient further attenuates to –1.8 percentage points per 10,000 CHF. This indicates strong cantonal heterogeneity—likely driven by differences in subsidy programmes, building regulations, and local energy infrastructure—that was previously confounded with the income measure. Within cantons, the income effect remains negative and significant, but is considerably smaller than the raw association suggests.

Two further findings deserve attention. First, share_pre1945 changes sign between M3 (–0.072) and M4 (+0.100): without canton fixed effects, municipalities with older building stocks tend to have fewer renewables; within cantons, the relationship reverses. This likely reflects that certain cantons combine old rural building stock with high wood heating penetration. Second, share_lowqual is significantly negative in M1–M3 but becomes insignificant in M4, suggesting that the data quality differential is primarily a between-canton rather than a within-canton phenomenon.

Coefficient Stability Plot

Figure X summarises the stability of the income coefficient across the four model specifications. The coefficient remains consistently negative across all specifications, with confidence intervals that never include zero. The point estimate shifts from –5.4e-06 in M1 to –1.8e-06 in M4, a reduction of approximately 67%, as urbanity, building structure, and cantonal heterogeneity are progressively absorbed by the controls. The widening confidence interval in M4 reflects the reduced within-canton variation available for identification after canton fixed effects are partialled out, but the effect remains precisely estimated and substantively meaningful.

Sensitivity Analysis: Including District Heating

As a robustness check, the main model specification (M4) is re-estimated with district heating included in the renewable category. District heating is excluded from the primary definition on the grounds that its adoption is structurally determined by local infrastructure availability rather than individual investment decisions. However, since district heating in Switzerland is predominantly fed by waste heat and biomass, its exclusion may understate the true renewable share in urban municipalities where district heating networks are most prevalent.

The income coefficient remains negative and statistically significant in both specifications (–1.8e-06 vs. –2.1e-06), and the direction of change is consistent with the expectation that urban high-income municipalities benefit most from district heating infrastructure: including district heating slightly strengthens rather than attenuates the coefficient, as these municipalities gain more from the expanded definition. All other coefficients remain stable in sign and magnitude across both specifications, with the exception of share_pre1945, whose coefficient increases from 0.100 to 0.14 when district heating is included — consistent with older urban building stock being disproportionately connected to district heating networks. The modest reduction in R² from 0.577 to 0.516 suggests that cantonal fixed effects explain somewhat less of the variation in the expanded outcome, likely because district heating penetration varies more within cantons than renewable heating in the primary definition. Overall, this robustness check confirms that the primary model results are not sensitive to the definitional boundary around district heating.

The canton-level subgroup analysis yields a striking finding that substantially enriches the interpretation of the national results. The income coefficient varies systematically with data quality across the three cantons, consistent with the hypothesis that measurement error in low-quality cantons attenuates the true income–renewables relationship.

In Basel-Landschaft, the canton with the best documented data quality (share_lowqual = 9.4%), the income coefficient is positive and significant (+4.9e-06, p < 0.01): within BL, higher-income municipalities have a higher renewable heating share, which is the theoretically expected direction. In Aargau, the low-quality comparison canton (share_lowqual = 60.9%), the coefficient is negative and significant (–1.7e-06, p < 0.05), consistent with the national estimate but smaller in magnitude. In Lucerne, the medium-quality canton, the coefficient is negative and larger in magnitude (–7.0e-06, p < 0.01), which suggests that structural canton-specific factors — likely the pronounced urban-rural contrast around the city of Lucerne — dominate the within-canton pattern independently of data quality.

The gradient from BL (+4.9e-06) to AG (–1.7e-06) to the national estimate (–4.2e-06) is broadly consistent with a data quality attenuation story: as measurement quality decreases, the income coefficient shifts in the negative direction. However, LU does not fit this gradient cleanly, which cautions against a purely data-quality-based interpretation. The divergence in LU is plausibly explained by the strong urban core of the city of Lucerne — a high-income municipality with low renewable share — creating a within-canton composition effect that resembles the national pattern.

The exceptionally high R² in BL (0.796 vs. 0.323 nationally) confirms that the model fits the high-quality data substantially better, consistent with reduced attenuation bias from outcome measurement error. The positive and significant share_lowqual coefficient in BL (+0.60, p < 0.05) — which is negative in all other specifications — further supports this interpretation: in a canton where data quality is generally high, the remaining low-quality entries likely represent municipalities with high renovation activity where new renewable systems were installed after the Volkszählung 2000 but not formally re-entered into the GWR, producing a spurious positive correlation between low-quality entries and renewable shares. In AG, by contrast, share_lowqual is strongly negative (–0.260, p < 0.001), indicating that in data-poor cantons, low-quality entries genuinely proxy for unrecorded fossil heating systems.

Taken together, the subgroup analysis provides suggestive evidence that the negative national income coefficient is a downward-biased estimate of the true relationship. In the canton with the highest data quality, income is positively associated with renewable adoption — consistent with the theoretical expectation that financial capacity facilitates investment in renewable heating systems. Resolving the ambiguity introduced by LU would require additional canton-level controls or a building-level analysis that directly links heating system records to owner income data.

The cantonal maps visualise the spatial distribution of renewable heating adoption and median income for the three focus cantons. Several patterns are immediately visible.

In Basel-Landschaft, municipalities with higher renewable shares are concentrated in the eastern and central parts of the canton, while the municipalities directly bordering Basel-Stadt in the northwest show lower shares. The income map shows the inverse pattern: the highest incomes are concentrated precisely in these northwestern municipalities. This spatial inverse relationship between income and renewables is visually consistent with the positive regression coefficient found for BL — within the canton, the high-income suburban municipalities close to Basel appear to be driving the positive association, while rural eastern municipalities combine lower incomes with higher renewable shares.

In Lucerne, the most striking feature of the renewable map is a single very dark municipality in the centre-south of the canton, indicating a renewable share well above 80%. The income map shows no corresponding income spike in the same location, suggesting this outlier is driven by local structural factors rather than income. The broader pattern shows higher renewable shares in the rural south and lower shares in the urban core around the city of Lucerne, while the income map shows the inverse — the city and its immediate surroundings have the highest incomes. This spatial pattern is consistent with the negative income coefficient found for LU.

Aargau shows a more uniform distribution in both maps compared to the other two cantons, consistent with its more homogeneous peri-urban character. Renewable shares are broadly in the 15–35% range across most municipalities, with isolated higher-share clusters in the northeast. The income distribution is similarly diffuse, with the highest incomes concentrated in municipalities bordering Zurich in the east. No strong spatial inverse pattern between income and renewables is immediately visible, consistent with the weak and only marginally significant income coefficient found for AG.

Conclusion

This study investigated whether a statistically measurable relationship exists between municipal median income and the share of residential buildings equipped with renewable heating systems across Swiss municipalities, and to what extent this relationship is robust to building stock characteristics and cantonal heterogeneity.

Regarding the first research question, the analysis finds a statistically significant negative relationship between municipal median income and renewable heating adoption across all model specifications. In the fully controlled model with cantonal fixed effects (M4), a 10,000 CHF increase in median municipal income is associated with a 1.8 percentage point reduction in the renewable heating share. This result is robust to the inclusion of district heating in the outcome definition and remains significant at the 0.1% level throughout. The negative direction of the effect runs counter to the intuitive expectation that higher financial capacity facilitates renewable investment, and is best understood as a composition effect: high-income municipalities are structurally urban, characterised by multi-family buildings and gas-based heating infrastructure, while lower-income municipalities are predominantly rural, where wood heating and heat pumps in detached single-family houses have long been the dominant heating form.

Regarding the second research question, the income coefficient attenuates substantially but does not disappear as controls are added. Adding building stock controls (M2) slightly amplifies the coefficient through a suppressor effect via share_efh, while adding municipality type and log population (M3) reduces it by approximately 22%, absorbing the urban-rural gradient. The most notable attenuation occurs when cantonal fixed effects are introduced (M4), where the coefficient reduces by a further 57% and the explained variance jumps from 32% to 58%. This indicates that a large share of the income–renewables association is driven by between-canton differences in subsidy regimes, building regulations, and energy infrastructure rather than by income per se. Within cantons, however, the negative income effect persists, suggesting a genuine structural pattern that is not fully explained by the controls available in this analysis.

The canton-level subgroup analysis provides important additional nuance. In Basel-Landschaft, the canton with the best documented data quality (share_lowqual = 9.4%), the income coefficient reverses sign and becomes significantly positive (+4.9e-06, p < 0.01): within BL, higher-income municipalities have a higher renewable heating share, which is the theoretically expected direction. The cantonal maps confirm this pattern spatially — high-income municipalities in the northwestern part of BL bordering Basel-Stadt show lower renewable shares, while the broader within-canton pattern points toward a positive income–renewables association once the suburban fringe effect is accounted for in the regression. In Aargau, the low-quality comparison canton (share_lowqual = 60.9%), the coefficient is negative but small and only marginally significant (–1.7e-06, p < 0.05), and the cantonal maps show no strong spatial pattern between income and renewables, consistent with the weak regression result. Lucerne does not fit the data quality gradient cleanly: despite medium data quality, the income coefficient is the most strongly negative of the three cantons (–7.0e-06, p < 0.01), likely reflecting the pronounced urban-rural contrast around the city of Lucerne rather than a data quality effect.

The gradient from BL (+4.9e-06) to AG (–1.7e-06) to the national estimate (–4.2e-06) is broadly consistent with the hypothesis that measurement error in low-quality cantons attenuates and ultimately reverses the true income–renewables relationship. The BL finding provides suggestive evidence that at sufficient data quality, income is positively associated with renewable heating adoption — consistent with the theoretical expectation that financial capacity facilitates investment at the point of the individual heating decision. Three limitations constrain the interpretability of these findings. First, the analysis operates at the municipal aggregate level, and the observed associations cannot be attributed to individual building owners, whose financial capacity is the theoretically relevant decision variable. Second, approximately 50% of GWR heating entries are flagged as low quality, likely leading to an underestimation of true renewable adoption rates and an attenuation of the estimated income effect — a concern partially addressed by the canton-level subgroup analysis but not fully resolved. Third, while cantonal fixed effects absorb time-invariant cantonal heterogeneity in subsidy programmes, they cannot account for within-canton variation in local incentive schemes or for changes in subsidy generosity over time, meaning the residual income effect identified in M4 may still partly reflect unobserved cantonal policy variation rather than a structural income constraint on renewable adoption.

Future research could address these limitations by working with building-level panel data that tracks heating system replacements over time, enabling a cleaner identification of the income effect at the point of the investment decision. Exploiting variation in cantonal and communal subsidy programmes as a quasi-experimental instrument would further strengthen causal inference. Such an analysis would require linking GWR building records to owner-level tax data — a data linkage that is technically feasible within the Swiss administrative data infrastructure but requires access beyond publicly available sources.
